title: What your house doesn't hold
hook: true Master, what is there that is not in Your house (Anand, opening pauris)

segments.voice: Yesterday, pauri two, man meriaa, and your line, stay with him. Did your mind wander, and did you bring it back? Today, pauri three asks a question about a house. Day three hundred eighty-four.

Some homes have a pantry that never seems to run out. You've maybe been in one. A grandmother's kitchen where, no matter how many people turn up, there's always more: another pot of dal, another stack of rotis, a box of sweets from somewhere. You arrive hungry and you leave carrying leftovers. You never once wonder whether there'll be enough. Pauri three of Anand Sahib asks a question about a house like that, except the house is God's, and the question is almost a laugh of wonder. Today: ghar terai.
screen: `A KITCHEN THAT NEVER RUNS OUT.` → `YOU LEAVE WITH LEFTOVERS.` → `A QUESTION ABOUT GOD'S HOUSE.`

segments.voice: It opens like this, in paraphrase: O true Master, what is there that is not in your house? Then: everything is in your house. In the original, the opening is saachiaa saahibaa, kiaa naahee ghar terai. True Master, what isn't in your home? It's a question that answers itself. Then the pauri says that the one who keeps your praise always, and holds your Name in their mind, finds the music of the Word playing within. And it closes by asking the question again: says Nanak, true Master, what is not in your house? Now, two things make this more than a nice sentiment. First, the word ghar, house or home. In Sikh scripture, ghar often means more than a building. It's the inner home too, the self, the heart, where the Guru teaches that the One is found. So the question works on two floors. Nothing is missing from God's house. And, the pauri hints, nothing is missing from the house within you, either, if the Name is living there. Second, look at who this is for. A lot of modern life runs on a quiet feeling of lack. Not enough time, money, love, energy, success. Advertising depends on it. Pauri three meets that feeling with a question. What is missing? Not, here's what you should want. Just: look around the house. What isn't here? The pauri also says something we'll stay with in a few days: that each person receives what the Master gives. For today, just the wonder. The house is full. Nothing is missing.
screen: `TRUE MASTER, WHAT ISN'T IN YOUR HOUSE?` · `GHAR: HOUSE, AND THE HOME WITHIN.` · `THE QUIET FEELING OF LACK.` · `LOOK AROUND: WHAT IS MISSING?` · then, large: `NOTHING IS MISSING.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: list what you already have. Sit and breathe slowly. Then, in your head or on paper, start a list of what's already in your house. Not just things. A roof. Water from a tap. A person who'd answer if you called. Your two hands. A memory you love. Today. Keep going until the list surprises you a little, until it's longer than you thought it would be. If you pray, you can say Waheguru after each one, or at the end. If you don't, just let the size of the list sink in. The bell holds the time.
Ghar terai, in your house. Pauri three: true Master, what is not in your house? Everything is there, and the same may be true of the home within.
Your line: nothing is missing. Today, when you feel the pinch of not enough, ask yourself the pauri's question, what is missing, and actually look. Day three hundred eighty-four.

howItsDone: Many Sikhs recite this third pauri as part of the short Anand Sahib sung at the close of services, and its opening question is often quoted as an expression of trust and contentment.

original.note: Gurmukhi: ghar terai, in your house; pauri three asks what isn't there.

trapdoor: what you thought: a line about God being rich.
what it means: a question that answers itself, nothing is missing from the Master's house, and maybe not from the home within.
what a scholar hears: ghar in gurbani often means the inner self as well as a dwelling, so 'kiaa naahee ghar terai' works on both levels, God's house and the heart where the Name lives.
